CPWD/PWD contractor registration is an administrative empanelment condition, not a statutory offence; non-compliance typically leads to blacklisting, de-empanelment or forfeiture of security deposit rather than a fine or imprisonment. Liable: contractor. [Knowledge-based]

Consequence of an incorrect/ineligible RoSCTL or RoDTEP claim (recovery with interest, and possible penalty under the Customs Act 1962/Foreign Trade Policy) was not independently confirmed with a specific section. Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Specific penalty for non-registration with the Textiles Committee under the Textiles Committee Act 1963 was not independently confirmed. Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Same as BIS Act general penalty - manufacture/sale of a QCO-notified textile product without the mandatory BIS mark is punishable with imprisonment up to 2 years or fine not less than Rs 2 lakh (Rs 5 lakh for subsequent contravention), and goods may be seized. Liable: manufacturer/importer. Basis: BIS Act 2016 s.17. [Search-confirmed - indiankanoon.org]

form_or_filing: Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory Use in Packing Commodities) Act 1987
obligation_register: Packing a commodity in contravention of the mandatory jute packaging order is punishable with a fine which may extend to double the cost of the jute packaging material that should have been used. Liable: packer/manufacturer. Basis: Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory Use in Packing Commodities) Act 1987 s.9. [Search-confirmed - indiacode.nic.in]

Discharging effluent in excess of standards, or establishing/operating an outlet without the Board's consent, is punishable with imprisonment for a term of not less than 1.5 years but which may extend to 6 years and with fine (enhanced for continuing contravention). Liable: occupier of the dyeing/processing unit. Basis: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974 s.41/s.44 (subject to decriminalisation of certain minor offences under the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act 2023). [Search-confirmed - indiankanoon.org]

Specific penalty for textile labelling non-compliance under the Consumer Protection Act framework was not independently confirmed as distinct from the general CPA offences (ss.88-89). Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Specific penalty for misuse of the Handloom Mark/Silk Mark under the Handlooms (Reservation of Articles) Act 1985 was not independently confirmed. Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Same as BIS Act general penalty - manufacture/sale without the mandatory ISI mark is punishable with imprisonment up to 2 years or fine not less than Rs 2 lakh (Rs 5 lakh for subsequent contravention), with seizure of goods. Liable: manufacturer. Basis: BIS Act 2016 s.17. [Search-confirmed - indiankanoon.org]

Manufacture/sale of a spurious or adulterated cosmetic is punishable with imprisonment up to 3 years and fine not less than Rs 50,000 or 3 times the value of the confiscated cosmetics (whichever is more); other cosmetics contraventions (incl. labelling) are punishable with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine up to Rs 20,000, or both. Liable: manufacturer. Basis: Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 s.27A/relevant offence section (Cosmetics Rules 2020 made thereunder). [Search-confirmed - medindia.net]

Failure to renew results in removal of the mark from the Register (loss of statutory protection), which is a civil consequence, not a penal offence; separately, falsely applying/using a trademark is punishable with imprisonment of 6 months to 3 years and fine of Rs 50,000 to Rs 2,00,000. Liable: trademark holder (for lapse); infringer (for false application). Basis: Trade Marks Act 1999 s.25 (renewal); s.103 (falsification). [Search-confirmed - indiankanoon.org, ipleaders.in]

description: Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements 2022
obligation_register: Non-compliance with CCPA directions is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months or fine up to Rs 20 lakh (s.88); causing a false/misleading advertisement is punishable with imprisonment up to 2 years and fine up to Rs 10 lakh, rising to imprisonment up to 5 years and fine up to Rs 50 lakh for subsequent offences (s.89). Liable: manufacturer/service provider/advertiser (and endorser in some cases). Basis: Consumer Protection Act 2019 s.88, s.89. [Search-confirmed - consumerprotection.in, ibclaw.in]

Specific penalty for breach of the (non-statutory) Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns 2023, as distinct from the general CCPA enforcement powers under CPA 2019 ss.88-89, was not independently confirmed. Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Failure to notify the CCI of a notifiable combination (or to furnish information sought during inquiry) is liable to a penalty which may extend to 1% of the total turnover, assets, or the value of the transaction, whichever is higher. Liable: acquirer/parties to the combination. Basis: Competition Act 2002 s.43A. [Search-confirmed - cci.gov.in, azbpartners.com]

acts_rules: State Shops and Establishments Acts (e.g. Delhi Shops and Establishments Act 1954)
obligation_register: Penalty for non-registration under State Shops & Establishments Acts varies by state; e.g. in Delhi the registration requirement itself has been kept in abeyance pending amendment of the Act, while other States impose fines (typically in the range of Rs 50-5,000). Liable: shop/establishment owner. Basis: State Shops and Establishments Acts (e.g. Delhi Shops and Establishments Act 1954). [Search-confirmed - labour.delhi.gov.in]

Penalty for failure to file the annual return under State Shops & Establishments Acts varies by state and was not independently confirmed for a specific state. Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

acts_rules: Consumer Protection Act 2019; Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020
obligation_register: Specific penalty for breach of the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020 (enforced through CCPA action, potentially attracting CPA 2019 ss.88-89) was not independently confirmed as a distinct provision. Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

description: Appoint; acknowledge in 48 hrs; resolve within 1 month
obligation_register: Specific penalty for failure to appoint a Grievance Officer under the E-Commerce Rules 2020 was not independently confirmed. Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Product liability under the Consumer Protection Act 2019 (Chapter VI, ss.82-87) is a civil remedy: a manufacturer, product seller or service provider found liable for harm caused by a defective/deficient product/service must compensate the claimant; it does not itself carry a criminal fine/imprisonment (separate CPA offences under ss.88-89 may apply for related misconduct). Liable: manufacturer/product seller/service provider, depending on the ground of liability. Basis: Consumer Protection Act 2019 ss.82-87. [Knowledge-based]

Specific penalty for breach of the Consumer Protection (Direct Selling) Rules 2021 (enforced by the State Government/CCPA under CPA 2019) was not independently confirmed as a distinct provision. Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Contravention of FDI/FEMA conditions (including sectoral conditions on retail FDI) is liable to a penalty up to 3 times the sum involved (or up to Rs 2 lakh where not quantifiable), plus a further penalty up to Rs 5,000/day for continuing contravention; the property/currency involved may also be confiscated. Liable: Indian entity/investee company receiving the investment. Basis: FEMA 1999 s.13. [Search-confirmed - taxguru.in]

Penalty for operating without a municipal trade licence is fixed under each State's/city's Municipal Act and varies by jurisdiction; not independently confirmed for a specific state. Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Manufacturing/packing/selling a pre-packaged commodity (including via e-commerce) that does not conform to the mandatory declarations is punishable with a fine up to Rs 25,000 for the first offence, up to Rs 50,000 for the second, and Rs 50,000-1,00,000 or imprisonment up to 1 year (or both) for subsequent offences. Liable: e-commerce seller/packer/manufacturer. Basis: Legal Metrology Act 2009 s.36. [Search-confirmed - indiankanoon.org]

Section 24 penalises contravention of s.22 (right to confer degrees) or s.23 (restriction on use of the word 'University'); institutions have been prosecuted under this section for unauthorised degree-granting, though the exact fine/imprisonment quantum was not surfaced in this session's search. Liable: unrecognised institution and its officers. Basis: UGC Act 1956 s.24. [Search-confirmed - casemine.com]

description: Proposed single regulator (HECI); status Needs manual check
obligation_register: The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill 2025 remains a proposed Bill and has not been enacted; no statutory penalty is currently in force under it (existing obligations continue under the UGC Act 1956). Liable: N/A until enactment. [Knowledge-based]

acts_rules: All India Council for Technical Education Act 1987
obligation_register: The AICTE Act 1987 does not appear to contain an explicit statutory fine/imprisonment section for operating an unapproved technical institution; enforcement is largely administrative (declaration as unapproved, withdrawal/denial of approval, referral to the State Government for civil/criminal proceedings under general law). Consult legal counsel for the applicable consequence. Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

NAAC/NBA accreditation is governed by UGC/AICTE guidelines rather than a standalone penal statute; non-accreditation itself carries no fine/imprisonment but can restrict eligibility for grants, higher fee/quota permissions, or foreign collaborations. Liable: HEI/institution. [Knowledge-based]

description: Admit 25% economically weaker in private schools
acts_rules: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009
obligation_register: Specific statutory penalty for non-compliance with the RTE Act's 25% economically weaker section reservation quota (as distinct from the general recognition-withdrawal provisions in ss.18-19) was not independently confirmed. Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Continuing to run a school after recognition is withdrawn (or without ever obtaining recognition) is liable to a fine up to Rs 1 lakh, and in case of continuing contravention, a further fine of Rs 10,000 for each day of continuance; prosecution requires prior sanction of an authorised officer. Liable: school management/person running the school. Basis: RTE Act 2009 s.18(5)/s.19(5). [Search-confirmed - indiankanoon.org]

UDISE+ data submission is an administrative MoE requirement; non-submission has no independent statutory fine/imprisonment but can affect access to central scheme funds/recognition. Liable: school/institution. [Knowledge-based]

description: UGC (Setting up of campuses of foreign HEIs) Regulations 2023
obligation_register: Specific penalty for operating a foreign HEI campus in India without UGC approval under the UGC (Setting up and Operation of Campuses of Foreign Higher Educational Institutions in India) Regulations 2023 was not independently confirmed. Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Failure to obtain/file the mandatory anti-ragging affidavit under the UGC Anti-Ragging Regulations can result in UGC withdrawing recognition/grants from the institution; the punishment for the act of ragging itself is separately provided under State anti-ragging laws and the general criminal law (IPC/BNS), not by non-filing of the affidavit per se. Liable: institution (for non-filing); individual perpetrator (for ragging). Basis: UGC Act 1956 (regulation-making power); State anti-ragging Acts. [Knowledge-based]

acts_rules: Guidelines for Regulation of Coaching Centres 2024
obligation_register: The Guidelines for Regulation of Coaching Centres 2024 are administrative guidelines rather than a standalone statute with its own fine/imprisonment provisions; enforcement mechanism and consequence for breach were not independently confirmed. Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

acts_rules: Income-tax Act 2025 (in force from 1-Apr-2026, replacing Income-tax Act 1961)
obligation_register: Consequence of loss/denial of tax exemption for a trust/society running an educational institution under the new Income-tax Act 2025 (effective 1 April 2026, replacing the Income-tax Act 1961) was not independently confirmed under the renumbered provisions. Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Originally, contravention (incl. operating without registration) was punishable with imprisonment up to 2 years for the first offence and up to 5 years for subsequent offences; the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act 2023 decriminalised this offence, replacing imprisonment with a monetary penalty and non-monetary measures (advisory, warning, censure). Liable: cable operator. Basis: Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act 1995 s.16 (as amended by the Jan Vishwas Act 2023). [Search-confirmed - pib.gov.in, forumias.com]

Suspension/cancellation of uplinking-downlinking permission by MIB for violation of licence conditions; permission is not a statutory licence so no separate court penalty, only administrative action. Liable: Broadcaster/channel company. Basis: MIB Uplinking/Downlinking Guidelines. [Knowledge-based]

First offence: imprisonment up to 2 years or fine up to Rs.1,000; subsequent offence: imprisonment up to 5 years or fine up to Rs.5,000; equipment seizure/confiscation for unregistered operation (imprisonment provisions largely decriminalised into monetary penalties/advisory-warning-censure by Jan Vishwas Act 2023). Liable: Cable operator/broadcaster. Basis: Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act 1995 ss.16-19 (as amended by Jan Vishwas Act 2023). [Search-confirmed - pib.gov.in, indiankanoon.org]

form_or_filing: IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021
obligation_register: Non-compliance with IT Rules 2021 due-diligence obligations causes the intermediary to lose safe-harbour protection under Section 79 IT Act 2000, exposing it to liability under IT Act/IPC for third-party content it hosts. Liable: Intermediary/platform (company) and its Grievance/Compliance Officer. Basis: Information Technology Act 2000 s.79; IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021. [Search-confirmed - mondaq.com, barandbench.com]

compliance_name: IT Rules Part III digital news publishers
obligation_register: Loss of safe-harbour exemption under Section 79 for non-compliance with Part III due-diligence code for digital news publishers, exposing the publisher to liability under applicable law and potential blocking under Section 69A. Liable: Digital news publisher/intermediary. Basis: Information Technology Act 2000 s.69A, s.79; IT Rules 2021 Part III. [Search-confirmed - mondaq.com, storyboard18.com]

No statutory penalty; ASCI is a self-regulatory body - non-compliance can lead to the ad being pulled down/modified on ASCI recommendation and referral to MIB/regulator (e.g. under Consumer Protection Act 2019 misleading ad provisions) but the ASCI code itself carries no legal sanction. Liable: Advertiser/agency. Basis: Self-regulatory ASCI Code; Consumer Protection Act 2019 (for misleading ads referred onward). [Knowledge-based]

description: Title verification; annual statement by 31 May
acts_rules: Press and Registration of Periodicals Act 2023
obligation_register: Penalty for publishing without registration up to Rs.5 lakh with direction to cease publication; continued default beyond 6 months or repeat unregistered publication can attract imprisonment up to 6 months; failure to file annual statement: penalty Rs.10,000-20,000 (first default), up to Rs.2 lakh for subsequent default. Liable: Publisher of periodical. Basis: Press and Registration of Periodicals Act 2023. [Search-confirmed - prsindia.org, indiacode.nic.in]

Imprisonment of 6 months to 3 years and fine of Rs.50,000 to Rs.2 lakh for knowing infringement of copyright (broadcast without licence); enhanced penalty (1-3 years, fine Rs.1-2 lakh) for repeat offence; offence is cognizable and non-bailable. Liable: Broadcaster/company and responsible officers. Basis: Copyright Act 1957 s.63. [Search-confirmed - indiankanoon.org, ssrana.in]

Imprisonment up to 3 years or fine up to Rs.10 lakh, or both, for exhibiting an uncertified film; continuing offence attracts further fine up to Rs.1 lakh per day; offence is cognizable and non-bailable. Liable: Exhibitor/distributor. Basis: Cinematograph Act 1952 s.7 (as amended by Cinematograph (Amendment) Act 2023). [Search-confirmed - indiankanoon.org, cbfcindia.gov.in]
Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Fine up to Rs.1 lakh for contravention of TRAI directions, Rs.2 lakh for second/subsequent offence, plus further fine up to Rs.2 lakh per day for continuing contravention; penalty adjudicated only by a Chief Metropolitan/Judicial Magistrate on TRAI's complaint, not by TRAI itself. Liable: Broadcaster/DTH/MSO/interconnect service provider. Basis: TRAI Act 1997 s.29. [Search-confirmed - scobserver.in, indiacode.nic.in]

description: Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act 2025
acts_rules: Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act 2025 (notified 22 Aug 2025); Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Rules 2026 (in force 1 May 2026)
obligation_register: Offering online money gaming: imprisonment up to 3 years or fine up to Rs.1 crore, or both; advertising such games: imprisonment up to 2 years or fine up to Rs.50 lakh; facilitating financial transactions: imprisonment up to 3 years or fine up to Rs.1 crore; repeat offence: imprisonment 3-5 years and fine Rs.1-2 crore; non-compliance with directions: civil penalty up to Rs.10 lakh plus suspension/cancellation of registration. Liable: Online gaming service provider/platform and its officers. Basis: Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act 2025 ss.5-10. [Search-confirmed - meity.gov.in, prsindia.org]

description: Act assented 18 Aug 2025, partly commenced 31 Dec 2025; NSB and NSBodies Rules 2026 notified
obligation_register: Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

form_or_filing: National Sports Governance (National Sports Bodies) Rules 2026
obligation_register: Non-compliance with athlete-representation/election norms can lead to non-recognition or withdrawal of recognition of the National Sports Body by the regulator, and disqualification of persons convicted of an offence with imprisonment from contesting elections. Liable: National Sports Body and its office-bearers. Basis: National Sports Governance Act 2025. [Knowledge-based]

Disputes not referred to/orders of the National Sports Tribunal not complied with can result in the Tribunal's civil-court-equivalent orders being enforced as a civil court decree; appeal lies to the Supreme Court within 30 days. Liable: National Sports Body/athlete/office-bearer. Basis: National Sports Governance Act 2025. [Knowledge-based]

Misutilisation or non-utilisation of SAI grants can lead to recovery of the grant amount, withholding of future grants, and blacklisting of the recipient body; action is administrative/contractual rather than a statutory court penalty. Liable: Grantee sports body/federation. Basis: Administrative - SAI grant-in-aid rules/General Financial Rules. [Knowledge-based]

Failure to file the annual list of managing body members can render the society and its office bearers liable to a nominal fine under the state amendment to the Act, and can affect the society's legal standing to sue/be sued; enforcement varies by state. Liable: Society/its office bearers. Basis: Societies Registration Act 1860 (state amendments) s.4. [Knowledge-based]

Consequences of an anti-doping rule violation include disqualification of results (forfeiture of medals/points/prizes), a period of ineligibility from competition/funding, provisional suspension, and financial sanctions including recovery of costs, as determined by the National Anti-Doping Disciplinary Panel. Liable: Athlete/athlete support personnel. Basis: National Anti-Doping Act 2022 s.6. [Search-confirmed - scconline.com, prsindia.org]

Late filing fee under section 234F (up to Rs.5,000) and penalty under section 271F-type provisions for non-filing; assessment/best-judgment assessment and denial of exemption where the society fails to file its return of income. Liable: Society (taxable entity). Basis: Income-tax Act 1961 ss.139(1), 234F. [Knowledge-based]

compliance_name: Advocates Act enrolment & BCI certificate of practice
description: Enrolment; BCI Bar Council of India Rules
acts_rules: Advocates Act 1961; Bar Council of India Rules
obligation_register: Practising without a valid Certificate of Practice/enrolment, or professional misconduct, can lead to disciplinary action by the State Bar Council/BCI ranging from reprimand to suspension from practice to removal of the name from the roll of advocates. Liable: Individual advocate. Basis: Advocates Act 1961 s.35. [Search-confirmed - indiankanoon.org, advocategandhi.com]

compliance_name: BCI Rules on foreign law firms
form_or_filing: BCI (Registration and Regulation of Foreign Lawyers) Rules 2022 (amended 2025 - Needs manual check)
obligation_register: Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Non-payment of Bar Council enrolment/welfare fund dues can lead to withholding or cancellation of the certificate of practice/renewal, restricting the advocate's right to practice. Liable: Individual advocate. Basis: Advocates Act 1961; Advocates' Welfare Fund Act 2001. [Knowledge-based]

Failure of verification/non-clearance of AIBE can result in suspension of the provisional enrolment/certificate of practice of the advocate by the Bar Council. Liable: Individual advocate. Basis: Advocates Act 1961; BCI Certificate and Place of Practice (Verification) Rules 2015. [Knowledge-based]

acts_rules: Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008; LLP Rules 2009
obligation_register: Penalty of Rs.100 per day of delay for the LLP and each designated partner, subject to a cap of Rs.1 lakh for the LLP and Rs.50,000 per designated partner, for failure to file the annual return (Form 11); no upper cap on the daily additional-fee accrual under the fee rules until paid. Liable: LLP and its designated partners. Basis: Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008; LLP Rules 2009. [Search-confirmed - taxguru.in, tallysolutions.com]

Additional fee of Rs.100 per day of delay in filing Form 8 (Statement of Account and Solvency), with slab-based higher additional fee for 'small' vs 'other than small' LLPs; continued default can attract penalty under the LLP Act besides the additional fee. Liable: LLP and its designated partners. Basis: Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008. [Search-confirmed - taxguru.in, setindiabiz.com]

compliance_name: LLP DIR-3 KYC for designated partners
obligation_register: Non-filing of DIR-3 KYC for a designated partner results in deactivation of the DIN/DPIN, with a late filing fee of Rs.5,000 payable to reactivate it. Liable: Designated partner. Basis: LLP Act 2008; Companies (Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Rules read with LLP Rules. [Knowledge-based]

Late filing of Form 3 (changes in partners/LLP agreement) attracts the standard additional fee of Rs.100 per day of delay under the LLP fee rules. Liable: LLP and its designated partners. Basis: LLP Act 2008; LLP Rules 2009. [Knowledge-based]

Failure to get accounts audited when turnover/contribution exceeds the prescribed threshold can attract penalty for non-compliance and additional fee on delayed filing of the audited Form 8; MCA can also initiate action for a false/inaccurate statement of accounts. Liable: LLP and its designated partners. Basis: LLP Act 2008 s.34 read with LLP Rules 2009 r.24. [Knowledge-based]

acts_rules: Chartered Accountants Act 1949; Peer Review Guidelines
obligation_register: Failure to comply with peer review requirements can result in the firm/member being denied empanelment for certain assignments and referral to ICAI's disciplinary mechanism, though peer review itself is largely a quality-assurance process rather than a penal one. Liable: CA firm/practising member. Basis: Chartered Accountants Act 1949; ICAI Peer Review Guidelines. [Knowledge-based]

Practising or signing reports without valid firm registration/UDIN generation is treated as professional misconduct, exposing the member to ICAI disciplinary action including fine up to Rs.5 lakh, suspension or removal of the name from the Register. Liable: CA firm/individual member. Basis: Chartered Accountants Act 1949; ICAI UDIN Guidelines. [Knowledge-based]

Practising without renewing the Certificate of Practice amounts to practising without a valid CoP, exposing the member to disciplinary proceedings under the Act besides the practice being void. Liable: Individual chartered accountant. Basis: Chartered Accountants Act 1949; CA Regulations 1988. [Knowledge-based]

Non-compliance with ICSI peer review requirements can affect empanelment/assignment eligibility of the practising firm and may be referred to the ICSI disciplinary mechanism for professional misconduct. Liable: CS firm/practising member. Basis: Company Secretaries Act 1980; ICSI Peer Review Guidelines. [Knowledge-based]

Practising without renewing the Certificate of Practice is treated as unauthorised practice, exposing the member to disciplinary action including removal of the name from the Register of Members. Liable: Individual company secretary. Basis: Company Secretaries Act 1980. [Knowledge-based]

Practising without renewing the Certificate of Practice is treated as unauthorised practice, exposing the member to disciplinary action by ICMAI including suspension/removal of the name from the Register. Liable: Individual cost accountant. Basis: Cost and Works Accountants Act 1959. [Knowledge-based]

NFRA can impose a monetary penalty (for individuals, not less than Rs.1 lakh, may extend to 5 times the fees received; for firms, not less than Rs.10 lakh, may extend to 10 times the fees received) and/or debar the auditor from practice for 6 months to 10 years for proven professional misconduct. Liable: Statutory auditor (individual/firm). Basis: Companies Act 2013 s.132(4). [Knowledge-based]

compliance_name: Legal notice to clients: GST for legal services
obligation_register: Failure to issue a proper GST-compliant legal notice/invoice, or wrongly claiming exemption on taxable legal services, can attract demand of tax with interest and penalty under the CGST Act for short payment/incorrect invoicing. Liable: Advocate/law firm providing taxable legal services. Basis: CGST Act 2017 ss.122, 73/74. [Knowledge-based]

description: Reporting for CA/CS/CMA in specified transactions
obligation_register: The Director, FIU-IND, may impose a monetary penalty of not less than Rs.10,000 but which may extend to Rs.1 lakh for each failure to comply with KYC/record-keeping/reporting obligations under PMLA on reporting entities/professionals covered as such. Liable: Reporting entity/professional (e.g. designated director/employee). Basis: Prevention of Money Laundering Act 2002 s.13. [Search-confirmed - indiankanoon.org, thelaw.institute]

Contravention of FCRA is punishable under specific sections (e.g. up to 5 years imprisonment for accepting foreign contribution without registration/prior permission under s.35); where no separate punishment is prescribed, residual penalty under s.37 is imprisonment up to 1 year or fine or both; FCRA registration/prior permission can also be suspended or cancelled. Liable: NGO/association and its office bearers. Basis: Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010 ss.35, 37. [Search-confirmed - taxtmi.com, fcraonline.in]

form_or_filing: Form FC-4 quarterly disclosure (exact form Needs manual check)
obligation_register: Failure to place mandatory quarterly receipt details on the organisation's website as required under FCRA Rules attracts a penalty of Rs.10,000 per violation under s.37 read with Rule 13. Liable: NGO/association. Basis: FCRA Rules 2011 r.13; FCRA 2010 s.37. [Knowledge-based]

Late/non-filing of the annual return FC-4 can lead to a penalty computed as a percentage of the foreign contribution received/utilised (typically 5% and escalating), and repeated default can lead to suspension or cancellation of FCRA registration and a bar on receiving further foreign contribution for up to 3 years. Liable: NGO/association. Basis: Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010; FCRA Rules 2011. [Knowledge-based]

description: Open FCRA account at SBI New Delhi
obligation_register: Receiving foreign contribution in an account other than the designated FCRA bank account (SBI, New Delhi branch) is a violation attracting penalty/compounding under FCRA and can lead to suspension or cancellation of registration. Liable: NGO/association. Basis: Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010 s.17; FCRA Rules 2011. [Knowledge-based]

acts_rules: Income-tax Act 2025 (in force from 1-Apr-2026, replacing Income-tax Act 1961); Section 12A/12AB provisions renumbered under new Act
obligation_register: Cancellation of 12A/12AB registration results in loss of exemption on income and taxation of accreted income at the maximum marginal rate; non-compliance can also trigger denial of exemption for the relevant previous year(s). Liable: Trust/institution. Basis: Income-tax Act 1961 s.12AB(4) (to be renumbered under Income-tax Act 2025 from 1-Apr-2026). [Knowledge-based]

Non-compliance with 80G conditions (e.g. non-filing of the statement of donations) leads to donors losing the deduction and can result in withdrawal/non-renewal of the 80G approval itself. Liable: Trust/institution (affects donors' deduction). Basis: Income-tax Act 1961 s.80G. [Knowledge-based]

frequency_or_trigger: Annual (one month before ITR due date)
obligation_register: Failure to obtain/file the audit report in Form 10B/10BB by the due date can result in denial of exemption under sections 11/12 for that year, taxing the entire income at normal rates (subject to condonation of delay by CBDT/PCIT in genuine cases). Liable: Trust/institution. Basis: Income-tax Act 1961 s.12A(1)(b). [Search-confirmed - incometaxindia.gov.in, taxguru.in]

Failure to furnish the statement of donations (Form 10BD)/certificate (Form 10BE) attracts a late fee of Rs.200 per day of default under section 234G and a penalty of Rs.10,000 to Rs.1 lakh under section 271K. Liable: Trust/institution. Basis: Income-tax Rules 1962 r.18AB; Income-tax Act 1961 ss.234G, 271K. [Knowledge-based]

A company/entity that undertakes CSR implementation without valid CSR-1 registration cannot be treated as an eligible implementing agency, and CSR spend routed through it may not count towards the funding company's mandatory CSR spend, exposing that company to CSR non-compliance consequences under section 135(7). Liable: Implementing agency/NGO. Basis: Companies (CSR Policy) Rules 2014. [Knowledge-based]

Failure to file CSR-2 (annexure to the annual return) attracts penalty for non-filing of financial statement/annual return particulars under the Companies Act, in addition to the substantive CSR non-compliance penalties under section 135(7). Liable: Company and its officers in default. Basis: Companies Act 2013 s.135; Companies (Accounts) Rules 2014. [Knowledge-based]

Failure to file annual returns/financial statements attracts additional fees and penalty under sections 92(5)/137(3) of the Companies Act on the company and every officer in default. Liable: Section 8 company and officers in default. Basis: Companies Act 2013 ss.92, 137. [Knowledge-based]

Contravention of the conditions of the section 8 licence can lead to the Central Government revoking the licence, and on revocation the company must add 'Limited'/'Private Limited' to its name and may be directed to wind up or amalgamate with a similar company. Liable: Section 8 company. Basis: Companies Act 2013 s.8(6). [Knowledge-based]

Non-registration/updation on NITI Aayog's DARPAN portal is largely an eligibility condition - non-compliance results in ineligibility to receive government/ministry grants rather than a direct penalty. Liable: NGO. Basis: Administrative - NITI Aayog DARPAN portal requirement. [Knowledge-based]

compliance_name: Trust annual filing with Charity Commissioner
acts_rules: Bombay Public Trusts Act 1950 and other state Acts
obligation_register: Failure to file the annual accounts/change report with the Charity Commissioner can attract a fine under the state Public Trusts Act and can result in the trustees being surcharged or the trust property being placed under greater scrutiny; specific fine amounts vary by state Act. Liable: Trustees of the public trust. Basis: Bombay Public Trusts Act 1950 (and corresponding state Public Trusts Acts). [Knowledge-based]

Failure to file the annual list of managing body members can render the society and its office bearers liable to a nominal fine under the applicable state amendment to the Act. Liable: Society/its office bearers. Basis: Societies Registration Act 1860 (state amendments). [Knowledge-based]

Late/non-filing of ITR-7 attracts late fee under section 234F and, where applicable, denial of exemption for that year besides interest under section 234A on any tax due. Liable: NGO/trust filing ITR-7. Basis: Income-tax Act 1961 ss.139(4A)/(4C), 234F. [Knowledge-based]

Failure to deduct/deposit TDS attracts interest under section 201(1A), disallowance of the expenditure under section 40(a)(ia), and penalty under section 271C equal to the amount of tax not deducted/deposited. Liable: NGO (as deductor). Basis: Income-tax Act 1961 ss.201, 271C. [Knowledge-based]

acts_rules: Code on Social Security, 2020 (in force 21 Nov 2025; erstwhile Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 and Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948 subsumed)
obligation_register: Delayed/non-payment of PF/ESI contributions for NGO staff attracts damages/interest under the Code, and criminal prosecution for repeat default can lead to imprisonment (up to 3 years for PF default) and fine up to Rs.1-3 lakh. Liable: NGO (as employer). Basis: Code on Social Security 2020 s.133 (subsuming EPF & MP Act 1952, ESI Act 1948). [Search-confirmed - taxmann.com, greythr.com]

acts_rules: Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act 2002; Amendment Act 2023
obligation_register: Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Failure to hold the AGM within the prescribed time can lead to the Central Registrar directing that the AGM be held, and office-bearers can be held liable for default under the Act's offences provisions. Liable: Multi-State Cooperative Society and its board. Basis: Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act 2002 (Amendment Act 2023). [Knowledge-based]

Failure to get accounts audited/file annual returns is an offence under the Act punishable with fine, and can also lead to supersession of the board by the Central Registrar in serious cases. Liable: Multi-State Cooperative Society and its officers. Basis: Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act 2002. [Knowledge-based]

compliance_name: MSCS election through Cooperative Election Authority
obligation_register: Failure to conduct elections through the Cooperative Election Authority as mandated can result in the Central Registrar superseding the committee of management and appointing an administrator pending fresh elections. Liable: Multi-State Cooperative Society and its board. Basis: MSCS (Amendment) Act 2023. [Knowledge-based]

Failure to get accounts audited as required attracts fine/penalty under the respective state Cooperative Societies Act and can also lead to surcharge proceedings against defaulting office-bearers. Liable: Cooperative society and its officers. Basis: State Cooperative Societies Acts. [Knowledge-based]

Failure to hold the AGM/conduct elections within time can lead to supersession of the managing committee by the Registrar of Cooperative Societies under the state Act and appointment of an administrator. Liable: Cooperative society and its board. Basis: State Cooperative Societies Acts. [Knowledge-based]

description: Banking Regulation Act as applicable to cooperative societies
obligation_register: Non-compliance with RBI directions/prudential norms by a cooperative bank can attract monetary penalty and, in serious cases, cancellation of the banking licence/supersession of the board by RBI. Liable: Cooperative bank and its board. Basis: Banking Regulation Act 1949 (as applicable to co-operative societies) s.46, s.36AAA. [Knowledge-based]

Wrongly claiming section 80P deduction where the cooperative society is ineligible results in disallowance of the deduction on reassessment, with interest and penalty for under-reporting of income under section 270A. Liable: Cooperative society. Basis: Income-tax Act 1961 s.80P; s.270A. [Knowledge-based]

The National Cooperative Policy 2025 is a policy/scheme document, not a statute, so non-adoption carries no direct legal penalty; it may affect eligibility for schemes/incentives linked to the policy. Liable: Cooperative societies (voluntary). Basis: Administrative [Scheme/Policy, not a statute]. [Knowledge-based]

Operating a food business (including a hotel/restaurant) without an FSSAI licence is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months and fine up to Rs.5 lakh under section 63; other quality/safety violations attract separate penalties up to Rs.10 lakh under sections 50-59. Liable: Food business operator (hotel). Basis: Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 s.63. [Search-confirmed - indiankanoon.org, taxclue.in]

Operating without a valid liquor/excise licence, or violating licence conditions, can lead to cancellation/suspension of the licence, seizure of stock, and prosecution with fine and imprisonment under the applicable state Excise Act. Liable: Licensee (hotel/restaurant/bar). Basis: State Excise Acts. [Knowledge-based]

Running an eating house without the mandatory police/local licence can lead to closure of the premises and prosecution with fine (and in some states imprisonment) under the applicable state Police Act/municipal law. Liable: Eating house owner/operator. Basis: State Police Acts / Municipal Corporation Acts. [Knowledge-based]

Operating without a valid Fire NOC can lead to closure orders/sealing of the premises by the fire authority/municipal body, and prosecution with fine under the state Fire Prevention and Life Safety Act. Liable: Hotel owner/operator. Basis: State Fire Acts (e.g. respective State Fire Prevention and Life Safety Measures Act). [Knowledge-based]

acts_rules: Immigration and Foreigners Act 2025 (in force 1 Sep 2025; Foreigners Act 1946 repealed)
obligation_register: Failure to submit Form C for a foreign guest can attract fine and, in serious/repeated cases, imprisonment for the hotelier under the general offences/penalty provisions of the Act; the foreigner may also face registration-related penalties. Liable: Hotel/guest-house operator. Basis: Immigration and Foreigners Act 2025. [Knowledge-based]

Non-registration under the State Tourism Trade scheme mainly results in ineligibility for tourism incentives/classification rather than a direct statutory penalty, as it is generally an administrative registration. Liable: Hotel/tour operator. Basis: Administrative - State Tourism Trade registration rules. [Knowledge-based]

Playing copyrighted music in a hotel/restaurant without a PPL/IPRS public performance licence is copyright infringement, punishable with imprisonment of 6 months to 3 years and fine of Rs.50,000 to Rs.2 lakh under section 63 of the Copyright Act. Liable: Hotel/restaurant operator. Basis: Copyright Act 1957 s.63. [Search-confirmed - indiankanoon.org, ssrana.in]

Short-payment or non-payment of GST on hotel accommodation/luxury tax attracts demand of tax with interest and penalty (up to 100% of tax in fraud cases, 10%/Rs.10,000 in other cases) under the CGST Act. Liable: Hotel operator. Basis: CGST Act 2017 ss.73/74, 122. [Knowledge-based]

Operating an eating house without the requisite trade licence can lead to closure and prosecution with fine under the applicable state/municipal law. Liable: Eating house owner/operator. Basis: State Acts / Municipal laws. [Knowledge-based]

Hotel star classification is a voluntary administrative scheme of the Ministry of Tourism; non-participation carries no statutory penalty but affects eligibility for classification-linked benefits. Liable: Hotel. Basis: Administrative - Ministry of Tourism Hotel Classification Guidelines. [Knowledge-based]

description: Replaces Foreigners Act 1946 etc.; status Needs manual check
acts_rules: Immigration and Foreigners Act 2025 (in force 1 Sep 2025; repealed Foreigners Act 1946, Registration of Foreigners Act 1939, Passport (Entry into India) Act 1920, Immigration (Carriers Liability) Act 2000)
obligation_register: General offences under the Act (e.g. failure to register a foreigner, non-disclosure of required information) attract fine and imprisonment as prescribed in the schedule of offences; entering/remaining in a restricted area without authorisation attracts imprisonment up to 5 years or fine up to Rs.5 lakh; using forged travel documents attracts 2-7 years imprisonment and fine of Rs.1-10 lakh. Liable: Foreigner/host establishment as applicable. Basis: Immigration and Foreigners Act 2025. [Search-confirmed - drishtiias.com, legalserviceindia.com]

description: E-way bill for goods over Rs 50,000
obligation_register: Transporting goods without a valid e-way bill (where required) can lead to detention/seizure of goods and conveyance, and a penalty equal to 100% of the tax payable (or 2% of goods value for exempt goods) for release, under the CGST Act/Rules. Liable: Transporter/consignor/consignee. Basis: CGST Act 2017 s.129; CGST Rules 2017 r.138. [Knowledge-based]

Incorrect classification/non-payment of GST on Goods Transport Agency services attracts demand of tax with interest and penalty under sections 73/74/122 of the CGST Act. Liable: GTA/recipient liable under RCM. Basis: CGST Act 2017. [Knowledge-based]

Contravention of the CBLR can lead to suspension or revocation of the Customs Broker licence under Regulation 17, besides a monetary penalty of up to Rs.50,000 on the broker (Rs.10,000 on a G-card holder) under Regulation 18; revocation requires a serious/substantive breach, not merely a procedural lapse. Liable: Customs Broker (licence holder). Basis: Customs Act 1962; Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations 2018, regns 14, 17-18. [Search-confirmed - taxguru.in, jurishour.in]

Violation of AEO programme conditions can lead to suspension or withdrawal of the AEO certificate/status by the jurisdictional Customs authority, resulting in loss of the associated trade-facilitation benefits. Liable: AEO-certified entity. Basis: Customs Act 1962; CBIC AEO Programme Circular. [Knowledge-based]

Contravention of bonded-warehouse licence conditions can lead to cancellation of the warehouse licence under section 58B and confiscation of improperly warehoused goods and penalty under sections 111-117 of the Customs Act. Liable: Licensee of the bonded warehouse. Basis: Customs Act 1962 ss.58, 58B, 117. [Knowledge-based]

compliance_name: Carriers Act 1865 / Carriage by Road Act 2007
obligation_register: Operating as a common carrier without a certificate of registration is punishable with the penalty prescribed under section 194 of the Motor Vehicles Act (competent authority may impose this on the carrier); registration can also be revoked for repeated consignor complaints not rectified within 30 days. Liable: Common carrier/goods transport operator. Basis: Carriage by Road Act 2007 s.24; Motor Vehicles Act 1988 s.194. [Search-confirmed - indiankanoon.org, indiacode.nic.in]

Overloading attracts a penalty of Rs.20,000 plus Rs.2,000 per excess tonne; refusal to allow weighment attracts a further fine of Rs.40,000; the consignor, consignee, transporter and driver can all be held equally liable for overloading offences under section 199. Liable: Driver/owner/transporter/consignor/consignee (jointly). Basis: Motor Vehicles Act 1988 ss.194, 199 (as amended 2019). [Search-confirmed - assettype.com, legalonus.com]

compliance_name: Multimodal Transportation of Goods Act 1993 registration
obligation_register: Undertaking multimodal transportation without registration as a Multimodal Transport Operator is punishable with fine under the offences provisions of the Act, and the MTO can also be denied the limitation-of-liability protections it confers if unregistered. Liable: Multimodal Transport Operator. Basis: Multimodal Transportation of Goods Act 1993. [Knowledge-based]

form_or_filing: Central Motor Vehicles Rules 1989 Ch. VIII
obligation_register: Transporting dangerous/hazardous goods without complying with prescribed safety/placarding requirements is an offence under the Motor Vehicles Act/Central Motor Vehicles Rules, attracting fine and, for repeat/serious violations, suspension of the driving licence or permit. Liable: Driver/transporter/consignor. Basis: Motor Vehicles Act 1988; Central Motor Vehicles Rules 1989 rr.129-137. [Knowledge-based]

description: Producers, importers, brand owners register on CPCB portal
obligation_register: Non-registration/non-compliance under EPR rules attracts Environmental Compensation levied by CPCB based on the unfulfilled obligation, in addition to criminal liability under the Environment Protection Act - imprisonment up to 5 years (extendable to 7 years for continuing/repeat contravention) or fine up to Rs.1 lakh, or both, with a further fine of Rs.5,000 per day of continuing violation. Liable: Producer/Importer/Brand Owner (PIBO). Basis: Environment (Protection) Act 1986 s.15; Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016. [Search-confirmed - sortconsultancy.com, climeto.com]

Failure to file the annual EPR return or meet recycling/plastic-collection targets attracts Environmental Compensation calculated by CPCB on the shortfall quantity, besides liability under section 15 of the Environment Protection Act. Liable: PIBO. Basis: Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 (amended 2022); Environment (Protection) Act 1986 s.15. [Knowledge-based]

Non-registration on the CPCB EPR portal for batteries attracts Environmental Compensation and liability under section 15 of the Environment Protection Act for the producer. Liable: Battery producer/importer. Basis: Battery Waste Management Rules 2022; Environment (Protection) Act 1986 s.15. [Knowledge-based]

Failure to meet battery-recycling/collection EPR targets or file the annual return attracts Environmental Compensation levied by CPCB, calculated on the cost of collection/processing of the shortfall quantity. Liable: Battery producer. Basis: Battery Waste Management Rules 2022. [Knowledge-based]

Non-registration under the E-Waste Rules attracts Environmental Compensation and liability under section 15 of the Environment Protection Act (imprisonment up to 5 years/fine up to Rs.1 lakh, or both, with additional daily fine for continuing default). Liable: Producer of electrical/electronic equipment. Basis: E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022; Environment (Protection) Act 1986 s.15. [Knowledge-based]

Failure to meet e-waste EPR collection/recycling targets or file the annual return attracts Environmental Compensation levied by CPCB on the unfulfilled quantity. Liable: Producer. Basis: E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022. [Knowledge-based]

An unauthorised e-waste recycler/dismantler is liable to Environmental Compensation and prosecution under section 15 of the Environment Protection Act, besides cancellation/suspension of its EPR authorisation by the SPCB/CPCB. Liable: E-waste recycler/dismantler. Basis: E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022; Environment (Protection) Act 1986 s.15. [Knowledge-based]

Non-compliance with tyre EPR obligations attracts Environmental Compensation on the shortfall and liability under section 15 of the Environment Protection Act. Liable: Tyre producer/importer. Basis: Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules 2016. [Knowledge-based]

Non-compliance with used-oil EPR/collection obligations attracts Environmental Compensation and liability under section 15 of the Environment Protection Act besides possible cancellation of the authorisation. Liable: Used-oil generator/producer. Basis: Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules 2016. [Knowledge-based]

Non-compliance with end-of-life-vehicle EPR obligations can attract Environmental Compensation and cancellation of the registered vehicle scrapping facility's/producer's authorisation besides liability under section 15 of the Environment Protection Act. Liable: Vehicle manufacturer/registered scrapping facility. Basis: Motor Vehicles (Registration and Functions of Vehicle Scrapping Facility) Rules; CMVR. [Knowledge-based]

compliance_name: Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 replaced by 2026 Rules?
description: SWM Rules 2026 status Needs manual check
acts_rules: Solid Waste Management Rules 2026 (notified, superseding Solid Waste Management Rules 2016, in force from 1-Apr-2026); Environment Protection Act 1986
obligation_register: Penalty provision not independently confirmed - consult legal counsel. [Needs manual check]

Non-compliance with mandatory plastic-packaging labelling requirements attracts Environmental Compensation and liability under section 15 of the Environment Protection Act, besides directions to stop production/sale of the non-compliant packaging by CPCB/SPCB. Liable: Manufacturer/brand owner using plastic packaging. Basis: Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 (amended); Environment (Protection) Act 1986 s.15. [Knowledge-based]

Failure to meet the prescribed battery-recycling targets attracts Environmental Compensation levied by CPCB, calculated on the basis of the cost of collection, transportation and processing of the shortfall quantity of waste batteries. Liable: Battery producer. Basis: Battery Waste Management Rules 2022. [Knowledge-based]
